title: Reduction of physiological stress by urban green space in a multisensory virtual experiment
research_question: To determine the potential stress induction and stress recovery of three multisensory environments (urban, park, forest) and to investigate how visual, auditory, and olfactory stimuli jointly enhance subjective experience and physiological stress reduction.

participants.description: 154 individuals (mean age 27-28, 18-50 years old, mixed gender) from Stockholm, Sweden. Participants self-declared health, normal vision/hearing/smell, not pregnant, and not using prescription medication.
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated beyond being from Stockholm.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Three 2D 360° Virtual Reality photos presented via Oculus Rift: (a) urban area in Stockholm (densely built up, no vegetation, commercial signs), (b) park in Uppsala (lawn, managed pine trees, distant buildings), (c) city forest in Uppsala (unmanaged, diverse foliage, dead wood).

Congruent auditory stimuli presented via earphones: urban (traffic noise, no voices), park (Willow warbler bird song, slight breeze), forest (nine bird species songs, slight breeze). Sound levels varied by 'location' (city: 57–79 dBA; park: 45-79 dBA; forest: 45-78 dBA).

Congruent olfactory stimuli presented via computer-controlled olfactometer: urban (diesel, tar, gunpowder), park (grass), forest (fir, European silver fir, mushroom). Odours presented birhinally every 5 seconds for 3 seconds.

mechanisms: The olfactory system has unique neural pathways, with receptors located only two synapses away from the amygdala and hypothalamus, allowing unfiltered access to these key nodes in initial stress responses.
Multisensory effects on stress reduction may be caused by associations between sensory stimuli and past experiences, rather than innately-derived mechanisms.
implementation_implications: Urban planners should consider multisensory qualities, especially olfactory and auditory stimuli, when planning open green spaces, not just visual stimuli.
Creating barriers that block noise in urban areas could facilitate the perception of natural sounds like bird songs, contributing to stress reduction.
Urban planners should consider a city's 'smellscape' to enhance well-being.

tables.description: Means (M) of skin conductance levels (µSiemens) in the different environments (Urban, Park, Forest) during Stress and Recovery periods, with standard deviations (SD).

Pleasantness ratings of environments and sensory stimuli (Visual, Olfactory, Auditory) for City, Park, and Forest environments, including average rating (M), standard deviation (SD), and significance (P) from pairwise Student's t-tests.

limitations: The study did not perform all possible stimulus combination iterations, making it difficult to statistically separate the importance of each of the three senses to the physiological response.
Participants were recruited from Stockholm, a highly urbanized area, and may have been habituated to city stress, potentially influencing their responses.
The majority of participants were young, and previous studies suggest older individuals may respond more negatively to noise, indicating potential age-related differences not fully explored.
The exact link between physiological stress responses and psychological stress is not fully known.
The experimental design does not allow for direct assessment of the link between environmental stimuli and long-term stress due to ethical considerations.
Due to multiple testing, the statistical threshold used was conservative, and results should be considered tentative without direct replication.
The use of 2D 360° VR photos, rather than 3D, may limit the ecological validity and potential for negative or positive interpretations related to distance.

paper_metadata.title: Reduction of physiological stress by urban green space in a multisensory virtual experiment
paper_metadata.publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Reduction of physiological stress by urban green space in a multisensory virtual experiment
paper_metadata.crossref_publisher: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractAlthough stress is an increasing global health problem in cities, urban green spaces can provide health benefits. There is, however, a lack of understanding of the link between physiological mechanisms and qualities of urban green spaces. Here, we compare the effects of visual stimuli (360 degree virtual photos of an urban environment, forest, and park) to the effects of congruent olfactory stimuli (nature and city odours) and auditory stimuli (bird songs and noise) on physiological stress recovery. Participants (N = 154) were pseudo-randomised into participating in one of the three environments and subsequently exposed to stress (operationalised by skin conductance levels). The park and forest, but not the urban area, provided significant stress reduction. High pleasantness ratings of the environment were linked to low physiological stress responses for olfactory and to some extent for auditory, but not for visual stimuli. This result indicates that olfactory stimuli may be better at facilitating stress reduction than visual stimuli. Currently, urban planners prioritise visual stimuli when planning open green spaces, but urban planners should also consider multisensory qualities.
